en: The Stage of Completion (*niṣpannakrama*):
The previously mentioned protections and so forth are not accomplished without the ultimate reality (*tattva*). As stated by the Blessed One in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-mahāyogatantra*:
Among the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma of the Great Sage, those who do not know that reality are all fruitless. Therefore, reality is introduced. What is that reality?
It is the bodhicitta, primordially unarisen and blissful, as stated by the Blessed One in the *Samājottara*:

In the *Vyākhyātantra*: "That which is without beginning or end, peaceful, the exhaustion of existence and non-existence, all-pervading, and inseparable from emptiness and compassion—this is known as bodhicitta. And since this is not accomplished apart from the purifications of body, speech, and mind, it is introduced [as follows]: therein, the practitioner...
Having removed ordinary ego-grasping through conviction in emptiness, [the practitioner] instantly [visualizes] himself in the form of Mahāvajradhara,
white in color, with two arms, and so forth. Thus is the yogi who performs the fourfold yoga.

Having thoroughly contemplated the world as having the syllable *hūṃ* at its core, and having seen that the world is that Vajrasattva born from it, one should proceed with that wisdom (*dhī*) according to the rule; thus it concludes. This refers to the unreality of the body of the Vajradhara, which consists of the realized mantra-nature.

Thoroughly understanding [the body] by way of its nature as being without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) is that "separation from the body" (*kāyaviveka*). Alternatively, it is the falsity (*alīkatva*) of the body due to the manifestation of the hundred families (*śatakula*); for according to scripture, "the families are said to be of a hundred kinds. Thus, its falsity is established through worldly convention alone, such as [the stages of] childhood, youth, and so forth.

Because the intrinsic nature of the [three] states is unapprehendable; therefore, through scripture and realization, the unreality of the body abiding in the three realms is "bodily isolation," just like that of a body submerged beneath the surface of water. It is "having *hūṃ* at its core" because it has arisen from the three syllables.
Having understood the falsity of the body, how could its cause—the three syllables—not be false? In this regard, it cannot be known without the sequential order of the reality of wind (*vāyutatva*).
The reality of wind is the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*); it [emerges] from the two nostrils by way of the sequence of the four mandalas.

Through the processes of entry (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and emergence (*vyutthāna*), there are sixteen hundred and twenty [cycles]. Regarding those [processes] such as entry and so forth, there is the recitation of the symbolic mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Through the meditation upon that, one should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose, and within that mustard seed, one should meditate upon the world with its moving and unmoving beings, and so forth.

Through the cessation of sixteen hundred million streams at the limit of excellence, there is the cessation even of the three syllables; thus, the unreality of speech is the isolation of speech (*vāgviveka*), like an echo. By this very sequence, for the mind associated with breath—which consists of the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping—its effect [is likewise ceased].
The discernment of the mind (*cittaviveka*) is the realization that even the one hundred and sixty innate dispositions (*prakṛti*), such as detachment, passion, and intermediate passion, are unreal,
just like the mind in a dream. Thus, through the second stage of vajra-recitation, [one realizes the unreality] of speech and mind.
Because of the thorough knowledge of the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvasvabhāva*), those very same sixty-two views and ninety-eight afflictions (*kleśa*),
though they arise, do not become causes for cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), because even these views and afflictions lack the nature of intrinsic nature. Indeed, these [do not exist].
The five aggregates at the moment of death produce an effect characterized by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);

however, for those who have obtained the instruction on self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), they produce an effect characterized by self-consecration. And that [self-consecration] cannot be known without the causes for the destruction and arising of the eight categories of reality (*aṣṭapadārtha*).

As the venerable Āryadeva stated: "The four [elements] beginning with earth, as well as the four voids—these eight categories should be known as the causes of destruction and arising. First, the sequence of their destruction is demonstrated:
the aggregate of form, whose nature is Vairocana, and those belonging to its family, such as Kṣitigarbha and the rest."
Having first gathered the earth, Locanā should go; Māmakī, whose nature is Ratnasambhava,
goes with the fire along with Vajrapāṇi and others of that family, while the fire itself...
Pāṇḍaravāsinī is the aggregate of perception whose nature is Amitābha, together with those belonging to his family.

Having taken up the olfactory faculty and so forth, it enters the wind element. The wind, moreover, is the nature of the *tārā* Aḥ, the accomplishment of the *siddhi*, and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) belonging to that family; having become one with the gustatory faculty and so forth, it proceeds toward the empty gnosis, the antidote to light. Furthermore, the empty...
Through the nature of detachment (*virāga*) and so forth, together with the counteragent of the appearance of light, the extremely empty gnosis (*atiśūnyajñāna*) proceeds;
that [gnosis] proceeds as the great empty gnosis (*mahāśūnyajñāna*), which is the counteragent of the attainment of light through the nature of passion (*rāga*) and so forth;
and the great empty [gnosis], by means of intermediate passion and so forth, enters into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

The noble Nāgabuddhipāda has also said: "When the four [elements] have become separate, the aggregate and likewise the sense-faculty dissolve in this sequence, just as they came before. First the earth goes to water;
water goes to fire; fire follows after wind; and wind [dissolves into space]."
One should enter into knowledge; having attained discernment and retention, one should then enter into the radiant light.

From that, having attained the state of a Gandharva, one is born impelled by karma. Thus, having come into being again and again within the oceans of birth, through the whirling of the whirlpools of primordial nature (prakṛti), [one remains].

The world does not attain the further shore. By this, the following is also explained: withdrawal, as well as meditation, breath-control, and concentration. Therefore, the Great Void is a limb of concentration; from that—
Thus, the triple emptiness arises; from that, emptiness [arises], and by this, recollection (*anusmṛti*) is explained.
Through the thorough knowledge of the non-duality of those two truths, there is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). It has been stated by the Illuminator (*Āloka-upadarśin*);
the state of sovereignty over the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvaratva*) has been established. Radiance (*ābhāsa*).
And according to the scripture, "One who sees the three [bodies] is established on the ten stages.

He who has received the instruction on the clear light through the sequence of self-consecration is adorned with all the qualities of a Buddha by means of the diamond-like samādhi on the stage of Buddhahood.
It has also been taught that one should remain throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) through union with the immeasurable goddess Viśvaramaṇī.

By means of the mere non-appearance of one's own mind, one attains the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-vihāra*). It is devoid of the yoga of the activity of arising; it is the samādhi resembling a vajra-image.
"Bodhisattvas attain that which conforms to the body of the Tathāgata," according to scripture. Thus,
having attained the thorough knowledge of body, speech, and mind as they truly are, sentient beings who profess [the efficacy of] karma [are liberated] from beginningless saṃsāra.
Due to the continuity of afflictions and karma arising from one's own conceptual constructions, like a silkworm,
one constructs for oneself a great mass of suffering through the succession of births; having experienced the ripening of the fruits of accumulated wholesome and unwholesome karma, once again—
Having abandoned the physical body through the sequence of the ultimate reality maṇḍala, [the consciousness] is comprised by the wind element,

associated with sensation, bound by craving, flowing forth from the dharma-realm, embraced by mindfulness, and associated with the preservation of wholesome and unwholesome [states], [consisting of] five or six...

The infant, resembling one year of age, possessing all sense faculties, subsisting on fragrance, and indestructible even by diamonds and other such things, endowed with the impetus of karmic supernatural power, remains for seven days in the interval between states; then,
being impelled by the wholesome and unwholesome karma arisen from its own conceptualization, and having encountered causes and conditions.
One takes rebirth again and again in the five destinies according to the analogy of a waterwheel and experiences the suffering of saṃsāra; therein, this is the sequence of rebirth:
first, when the knowledge of means and the knowledge of wisdom have arisen from the intermediate state (antarābhava).

When the mother is healthy and in her fertile period, and both parents are mutually affectionate— having observed this mutual passion and through the grasping of desire— one leaves the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), enters through the crown of the head (*vairocana-dvāra*),
attains the ground of gnosis (*jñāna-bhūmi*), and [abides in] the subtle element.
Through that entry, it arises. From fire comes water; from water, earth is born.
Thus, having both been liquefied by the bliss of supreme joy and having become mixed with semen and blood, it falls into the midst of the womb in the form of a drop. This is the meaning.

It illuminates [the following]: "In the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Mahāyogatantra*, it is said that he dwells within the wombs (*bhaga*) of the vajra-women of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. Thenceforth, he develops in stages:
first in the form of the *kalala*, then the *arbuda*, from which the *peśī* is born, and then the *ghana*."

And from that embryo, being further impelled by the vital air (vāyu), there arise the fivefold types of swellings in the form of primary and secondary branches; from those, the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth, as well as the sense organs, physical forms, and minor characteristics, are produced in due order. Thus.

The placement of Akṣobhya and the others in the stages of the embryo (kalala) and so forth, according to the sequence of the arising of existence, is to be understood from scripture. Therefore, having diligently mastered the procedure for body, speech, and mind, and having properly propitiated the Vajra Guru, one becomes oriented toward self-consecration.

Thus it occurs. Having attained isolation of body, speech, and mind through this sequence, and having received the permission of the satisfied Guru, one should perform a great feast-offering (*gaṇapūjā*) and offer a sixteen-year-old girl to the Vajra-Guru. This is preceded by the initiations of the garland, water, and so forth, within the colored powder mandala and other such settings.

Having attained physical isolation and, through the secret initiation, having achieved verbal isolation, one likewise attains mental isolation; for the mind is thoroughly mixed with the wind in its subtle form.

The scriptural authority begins with the words "It has gone," and so forth. The venerable Āryadeva also stated in the *Vāgviveka* that without the purification of speech, the purification of the mind cannot be accomplished. Therefore, through the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) alone, there is the purification of both. In this regard, the sequence for the secret initiation is as follows, from the evening...

Having bestowed the authorization for the master— including the garland, water, the fully awakened ones, the vajra, the vajra-bell, the mirror, and the name— the Guru should consecrate the disciple with the secret consecration at midnight.
Thereafter, he should offer to the Guru a consort (*prajñā*) whose youth has not yet declined.

Then the Guru, having formed the *pañcakula-kalāpinī* [mudrā] and experienced the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*), which is the state of purification from the afflictions through the sequence beginning with detachment (*virāga*), takes the bodhicitta situated within the lotus of the mudrā; then, having bound the face-cloth with his thumb—

One should cause it to fall into the mouth of the disciple by means of the two ring fingers. The disciple, for his part, should consume it while thinking, "I satisfy all the Tathāgatas residing within my own body. Furthermore, with the bodhicitta thus taken up, [one should offer] the conch and so forth.

Having stirred the standing fragrant water and preceded by auspicious verses, the Guru should consecrate the disciple. As stated by the Blessed One in the *Guhyendutilaka*: "Having cast [the disciple] from the center of a lotus blazing with jewels, with his form completely dried, he should sprinkle him upon the stainless heads of all the Jinas."

"With showers of jewels and the waters of the wisdom arising from pure vajras"—having thus received the secret empowerment, one should praise the Guru for the sake of the instruction on self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) by means of his truly existing qualities with this king of hymns: "There is no impurity in your body; there is neither flesh, bone, nor blood."
You have manifested a body like a rainbow in the sky.

Although there is no impurity in your body and no arising of hunger or thirst, you displayed worldly activities for the sake of conforming to the world. All phenomena are to be grasped as being like the moon reflected in water.

Unreliant, free from egoism, free from delusion, and without support—homage be to you! You are always in a state of meditative equipoise while walking, standing, and likewise sleeping; in all modes of conduct, you are without support—homage be to you!

You manifest through great miraculous power by means of the illusion-like samādhi; having attained the state of non-differentiation, you are without support—homage be to you! Then the Vajra Guru should bestow the self-consecration, like a reflection appearing in a stainless mirror.
That knowledge which is revealed by the true Guru— namely, the self-established (svādhiṣṭhāna),

free from existence and non-existence, the antidote to ignorance, possessing a form that is never-failing, consisting of the three appearances, having a nature indivisible from the unreal body and so forth, and which is to be personally realized within the continuum of the disciple— that is it.

The form of the deity, which is beyond perception, is here faultless and characterized by illusion; designated as "the perception of light," it is illustrated by the twelve examples of illusion. Furthermore, this is the mind-made body (*manomaya*) of the Buddhas.

Regarding the body, it has been said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna: Just as a reflection is clearly seen in a stainless mirror, Vajrasattva— liberated from existence and non-existence— is beautifully depicted, endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
He whose form is unsurpassed should show it to his own disciple; that is called self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna).

Illusion itself is the truth of the conventional; that is the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*). That very [illusion] would be the *gandharva*-being, and so forth in detail. How is it composed of bliss? Because its light is perceived without distinction from the cognition that takes other forms and so on as its objects; it is indeed true, but—

There is a distinction regarding the object of the touch of the illusion of woman (*strīmāyā*), because therein the clear manifestation of the blissful differentiation of the three knowledges (*jñāna*) proceeds. This can be demonstrated here as well by that example, on account of its being like an illusion (*māyopama*).
As it has been stated in the *Sarvaśuddhiviśuddhikrama*:

"Of all illusions (*māyā*), the illusion of woman alone is preeminent. This distinction of the three types of knowledge is clearly perceived right here: passion, dispassion, and that which lies between the two."
From the union of the two organs, there is the meeting of the vajra and the lotus;

the union of the two gnoses is proclaimed as "attainment" (samāpatti). Through the attainment of the two gnoses by means of the performance [of the ritual] as described, that gnosis which is attained with effort—
That is the attainment of light. He for whom the union of the vajra and lotus does not exist even conventionally,
yet has experienced it even once through the power of yoga— having understood its differentiation, the yogi,
by the very nature of the activity of gnosis, should constantly characterize that very primordial nature.

Furthermore: how, then, is a mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) endowed with all characteristics, such as hands and feet, produced by mere cognition alone? Since the mind is devoid of color, shape, and so forth, that is true; however, because the mind is accompanied by subtle elements (dhātu), it [manifests] in the form of a deity endowed with all characteristics.
And it is said in the Sūtra: "The mind is devoid of color and shape, its nature is equal to space, and like ultimate truth, it is difficult to perceive;
however, there is the appearance of the three lights, because the wind element is formless."

And consciousness (*jñāna*) is formless; for this very reason, it is joined with the wind and with consciousness. Therefore, the manifestation of light (*ālokopalabdha*), which consists of the three appearances, accompanied by the five rays and endowed with all the qualities of a Buddha, arises as the illusory form of the deity.

For this very reason, those engaged in the systems of the Sūtras and other scriptures, as well as practitioners of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), describe illusions, dreams, and so forth as metaphors. Yet they do not understand that the metaphorical nature refers to the instruction on self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). And it is stated in the *Karmāntavibhāga*: "The thorough knowledge of appearances."
It is beyond the reach of logicians, and even the convergence of appearances is extremely difficult to attain. Others conceptualize it as passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and goodness (sattva);
yet these are merely the three appearances resulting from the loss of knowledge of one's own true nature, and they serve as the cause for both worldly existence and nirvāṇa.
This is considered the threefold knowledge; wherever the natures of appearances reside, there lie merit and demerit.
For one whose three appearances are purified, the state of the Sugata is certain—[the state] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and whoever else [there may be].

Kapila and others were utterly deluded regarding the manifestation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), as well as regarding purification in every respect. Therefore, that which must be stated according to our view is this: without the body, knowledge does not arise; without knowledge, the body does not exist.
For this very reason, [the Buddha] has a nature consisting of the realization of the Body of Knowledge (*jñānakāya*), which takes the form of a false body.

It does not have the nature of self-awareness, because there is no form of its own distinct from the form of the object of perception. That very cognition of the [object] is metaphorically termed "self-cognition. It arises in the form of three appearances. Its own substratum consists of bliss. This meaning is illuminated in the Root Sūtra.
"May you generate the mind in the form of the body, the body in the form of the mind,
and the mind through the utterance of speech. Thus, this consciousness, having abandoned the body as its first manifestation,
takes the form of a drop (*bindu*).

That which is called the "intermediate state" (antarābhava) for ordinary beings is caused by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); however, for those who have received the instructions of all the Buddhas,
that very same thing is designated as "self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), just like [the reflection] existing within a mirror.

Knowledge is perceived from a painted cloth; in the same way, the self is manifested with the nature of a vajra-body, its limbs adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and—in brief—adorned with all the qualities of a Buddha. By this method...

Because the wind element and consciousness are formless, the consciousness element becomes thoroughly blended— like ghee poured into ghee— and performs all mundane and supramundane activities, as it is said in the *Anuttarasandhi*: [text omitted].

Knowledge is mere consciousness, devoid of characteristics like space; nevertheless, it has divisions consisting of twilight, night, and day. It is said that there are "light," "manifestation of light," and likewise "attainment of light. Its support is described as knowledge in the form of subtle wind.
Having become thoroughly mixed, it issues forth through the pathways of the senses and takes hold of sense objects.

When the wind, joined with the manifestation (*ābhāsa*), becomes the vehicle, it then sets all those constituent natures (*prakṛti*) into motion, whether in their proper order or in disorder. Wherever the wind is situated, it carries forth that very nature. Thus [is the process] regarding the manifestation of the three types of cognition and the constituent natures.
Because the elements of air, as well as their functions, are formless, there is no mutual differentiation among them.

It has been stated by the Blessed One that [all things] are empty; how then is that mind-made body bound by wholesome and unwholesome karma? Furthermore, within the beginningless wheel of existence, that which has been accumulated—whether wholesome or unwholesome—by means of these one hundred and sixty primary natures (prakṛti), [is what constitutes bondage].

In this very life, [the mind] arises and perishes moment by moment; how then could it be perceived in other births? Because of their failure to fully understand this intrinsic nature, one remains unliberated—of this there is no doubt. For the natures of the auspicious and inauspicious are empty.
Arising from the three [realms] by the power of the wind-vehicle, they are born moment after moment, experience sense objects again and again,
and repeatedly enter the clear light, as it is said in the *Anuttarasandhi*:
Just as many clouds, appearing in various shapes and colors,
arise from the expanse of the sky and indeed dissolve back into it,
so too do all the constituent elements (prakṛtis), which have the three appearances as their cause.
Having experienced all sense objects, they enter the luminous state.

Thus, due to the non-recognition of their own nature, veiled by the cataract of ignorance, they perform virtuous and non-virtuous actions and wander through the five realms of existence. Having committed the immediate transgressions and so forth, they do not—
[Evil] ripens in the hells; having performed auspicious acts such as giving, one is honored in the heavens and other celestial realms.

Having undergone this again and again throughout thousands of endless births, one grieves out of delusion, thinking, "This is the ripening of my past karma. Knowing that very thing by which beings are afflicted through the union with the light of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), [one should realize it].

"The wise are liberated from the cage of existence. And likewise, it is said in the *Guhyakośasūtra*: "One has faith in and resolves upon all phenomena as primordially pure; for such a being, I declare there shall be no going to the lower realms. Why is that? Because there is none..."
The state of being a mass of afflictions is as follows: indeed, all afflictions arise through the conjunction of the totality of causes and conditions; and as soon as they have arisen, they cease.
That which is their arising is itself the destruction of the afflictions; this is what is meant by that.
Having awakened the disciples through reasoning and the realization of scripture,

and having established the purification of virtuous karma through the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature of the afflictions according to the sequence of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna-krama*), [he also taught] self-consecration itself.

Having purified [the mind] by means of luminosity and then demonstrated the emergence from it, one establishes [the practitioner] in the samādhi of the "yoked pair" (yuganaddha); this is the stage of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhānakrama).

In accordance with the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the body is unreal; it is characterized by being produced through the three vajras and is merely a matter of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). Therefore, within the body, the form of the primordial deity endowed with the excellence of all aspects is not perceived.
Because the body is merely an aggregate of atoms, the thorough knowledge of speech— through the sequence of entry and so forth— is likewise nothing more than vajra-recitation.
Even there, there is no form of a deity, because its intrinsic nature is like an echo.

The thorough knowledge of speech and mind is that they are merely appearances by their very nature; even therein, the form of the deity, which is like a vajra-image, is not apprehended, because the mind is a mere appearance characterized as the illusion-like indivisibility of the three vajras.

Even in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* [stage], there is no form of a deity adorned with powers (*bala*), superknowledges (*abhijñā*), masteries (*vaśitā*), compassion, and skillful means (*upāya*). Because it is purified by the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), it is the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*: "Even one who has entered the illusion-like samādhi... up to the point where he [perceives] others...
As long as one does not attain the realization of ultimate truth, one is not irreversible;

therefore, as long as there is conceptualization of consciousness regarding the three pure appearances, there is a continuity of afflictions, and from the continuity of afflictions comes rebirth. Even in the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), [rebirth] is not yet found.
The form of the deity endowed with the excellence of all aspects is entirely empty because of its universal emptiness; therefore, it is all-empty.
Having established that the characteristic is self-cognized luminosity, [one then proceeds] from the nature of emergence therefrom.

He establishes [the disciple] in the samādhi of the unified pair (*yuganaddha*). Regarding the characteristic of the non-duality of the two truths, this is the sequence: when the sun has set, having bestowed the *mālā* and other initiations with whatever requisites are available, one should bestow the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) at midnight.

In this sequence, having propitiated the Vajra-guru with material requisites such as forms and so forth, the disciple should offer to that guru a well-trained mudrā. Then the guru should bring about the arising of the manifestation through the ritual procedure of meditative union (*samāpatti*). And then the *kala*...

At midnight, the Guru, with a mind established in the *śādi* [stage] of bodhicitta, should consecrate his disciple with the secret empowerment (*guhyābhiṣeka*). Having received the empowerment, at the time of dawn, the disciple, with palms joined in reverence, should again propitiate the Guru with hymns of praise: "O you who are liberated from the three realms, equal to space..."
You have gone;

you do not burn in desires, O supportless one—homage be to you! Grant me, O Great Vajra, the purification of body, speech, and mind, which is without beginning or end, peaceful, and the purifier of all afflictions.
Thus propitiated by the recitation of his truly existing qualities, the yogin, having generated compassion for the disciple,
should then begin the sequence as follows: when the portion of the night has passed,
having reached sunrise and transcended the morning twilight— at this very moment, according to the perspective of external perfect awakening.

One seeks the inner awakening as it is stated in the Āgama: "The light of the night is the portion of darkness; the light of day is the radiance of the sun's clear rays. This [light] obtained during the twilight is repeatedly joined with its own inherent natures; it is not night."

Nor does it exist at twilight, nor during the day; he who is liberated by nature would be that moment of awakening spoken of as supreme by the Guru, accessible only to yogins. In which [moment] the nocturnal darkness is destroyed, everything has vanished, and the light of twilight has ceased, the sun shines forth.

As long as this stainless moment does not arise, the preeminent teacher may show the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) to the disciple; yet, once the darkness has been destroyed by the vision of external awakening,
one attains in a single moment the internal bliss of the Buddha’s enlightenment, free from all defilement.
Having thus established the external illustration of the fourfold emptiness, one should now demonstrate the internal awakening, characterized by personal realization, through this sequence.
This is the sequence:
First, one should see the appearance of a mirage, a mass of five-colored rays; second, the appearance of light, resembling moonbeams; third, the appearance of luminosity, resembling sunbeams;
fourth, the appearance of darkness, which is the perception of light. Then, in an instant, when that darkness has vanished—

One should behold with the eye of wisdom that which is luminous, exceedingly pure, having the nature of constant light, and characterized as ultimate truth. Having thus directly realized universal emptiness, one should take recourse in the two types of meditation. By this—

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: just as a drop of water dissolves gradually into pure water in a river or a lake, so too is the dissolution of the elements taught by the Lord of Yogins to occur perpetually and sequentially; and likewise, the destruction of the abode of the mirror occurs through a gradual process.

In the same way, those who follow the ritual procedure perceive it as the "grasping of the mass" (*piṇḍagrāha*); thus they imagine the sequence. Then, the Vajra-disciple, having attained the two types of meditation through the instruction on the desire for the two kinds of perfect enlightenment, holds his hands joined in a handful of flowers and becomes smiling-faced.

With the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), he requests the Vajra Master for the purpose of receiving the instruction on luminosity (*prabhāsvara*): "Therefore, O Great Lord, grant me the vision of perfect awakening, which is liberated from birth through karma and devoid of the three appearances. Then the Vajra Master...
[As if looking at the disciple, one should bestow the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) for the sake of the ultimate reality with this verse:
"Free from all entities, devoid of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and abandoned by the grasped and the grasper."
"By means of the equality of the selflessness of phenomena, one's own mind is primordially unarisen and has emptiness as its intrinsic nature.
[And thus, by means of the Jewel of Exegesis, one should establish luminosity; that which is the purification of the threefold emptiness is what is here called luminosity.]

That is the state of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyapada*), and that arises from the purification of the three types of gnosis (*jñānatraya*). That state of purified gnosis is reality (*tattva*), which is omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), unsurpassed, changeless, without appearance, free from duality, and supreme bliss (*paramaśiva*). This is also stated in the *Guhyendumaṇitilaka-yogatantre*:
"Beyond the cultivation of all limbs, free from conceptual construction and its objects, transcending measure and the bindu— this is the supreme maṇḍala.
This is stated in the *Lalitavistara*, a Mahāyāna sūtra, for one who desires perfect awakening.

Out of the conceit that the Tathāgata Śākyasiṃha would attain Buddhahood through the "Great Emptiness," he sat on the bank of the river Nirañjanā and entered the *āsphānaka* concentration. At that time, the Victors, filling the midst of space like sesame seeds in a pod, spoke with a single voice:

The two Victors call that "the taste" [of the moment] of a finger-snap; yet this meditation is impure and does not lead to the desired goal. By taking as one's object the supreme luminosity, which is like the expanse of space, once the state of luminosity is attained, you are born with a form according to your own will, and then all sovereign powers [are yours].

"Having attained the vajra-body, you shall rejoice. Having heard that sound, the Son of the Jina then released his bowstring; at the hour of midnight, he took hold of the reality (tattva) itself—neither with a straight body nor even with a crooked one, neither with breath nor without breath.
Neither silent nor even non-silent, neither with eyes opened nor with eyes closed,
he then beholds that manifest, all-wondrous, great knowledge which is pure and clear, through the grace of the Guru’s feet.

One who maintains pure clarity should, in a single instant, behold the entirety of the three times— the future, the past, and the present— as luminous. Adorned with the qualities of illusion such as the moon in water or a mirage,
one should sit at the time of sunrise in the diamond-like samādhi.

At the root of wisdom, he performed the shattering of Māra. Having attained the unsurpassed knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), the Lord of the Śākyas demonstrated that very same thing here for the sake of the welfare of the three worlds. What is called "knowledge of reality" is the vision of perfect awakening (abhisambodhi).

Even a person who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution and possesses little merit, by the grace of the Guru, obtains another wish-fulfilling gem; perform your practice as you desire, for he is the Perfectly Awakened One of the future.

It is also stated in the *Paramādya*: "The purification of passion and the other afflictions which is demonstrated in the *Paramādya* was likewise taught by the Tathāgatas with reference to universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnya*). Whatever reality is shown in various sūtras and tantras, this is indeed the state of universal emptiness, and nothing else."

In this regard, it is said: Within the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage, that which is the most essential of the essential has been proclaimed—the characteristic of perfect enlightenment. Whether one has matted hair, is naked, is shaven-headed, or wears a topknot, one should live a life free from attachments.

Through various diverse signs, those who desire full awakening follow a sequence of practices such as vows and observances; yet, because they are devoid of reality, liberation is not attained by them due to their lack of knowledge of reality. And it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna: "That which exists or does not exist..."

That which is free from conventional expression, neither of the nature of merit nor of the nature of sin, and not consisting of both merit and sin—the Buddhas proclaim that as the supreme state of universal emptiness. Having attained such a reality, the yogi becomes the soul of all moving and unmoving things, the sole kinsman of the world; he who thus wanders [through existence].
The Lion of Men consists of gnosis; having attained the unmanifest body, he pervades the entire world. Thus is the sequence of luminosity.

Now, the stage of simultaneous union (*yuganaddha*), characterized by the non-duality of the two truths and free from all dualities, is introduced. Furthermore, conventional truth has been established through twelve analogies;
it is self-cognizable and beyond objective apprehension.
Having entered the deity-form, which is ultimate truth, unstruck (*anāhata*),
unassailed, the universal void, without increase or decrease, utterly pure, equal to space, and of stainless nature—
having thus entered the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) and become devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), who...

Who is it that arises? Who is it that, by means of the process of simultaneous union (*yuganaddha*), experiences true bliss as long as *saṃsāra* lasts? Who is it that becomes irreversible? For what purpose is liberation, and from what is one liberated?
Such is the question. Here, in the Vajrayāna, by means of the direct realization of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the eighth ground—
Having attained rebirth in the happy realms again and again,

one should continue to propitiate a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) according to the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Tantra* until one attains the stage of the completion process (*niṣpannakrama*), even if one has already achieved the isolations of body, speech, and mind.

Having attained the ten stages, one obtains the illusion-like samādhi. Having realized that, one attains the purification of appearances. Emerging from the state of non-appearance, one gradually manifests the Buddha-body, which is characterized by the union of the two aspects.
Having attained the vajra-like samādhi, he dwells adorned by all the Buddhas. By this method, through the sequence of manifest enlightenment,
one who has received the instruction on luminosity directly perceives the body, speech, and mind as being of stainless nature, because they are entirely empty.
Purified by the three knowledges, having the nature of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
it is neither thought nor silence; that too is the realm of nirvāṇa,
previously unexperienced and difficult to touch, liberated from karma and birth, the luminosity of the three appearances.

The state (*bhāva*) is extremely clear. From that clarity arises the great emptiness whose nature is the twilight. From that clarity, by the power of the illumination of the sun’s rays, there is the cool-natured illumination of the moon’s rays.
The arising of the knowledge of emptiness occurs. Therefore, the light, unified with the fourfold emptiness, appears like a mass, in the form of a firefly, illuminating all world-systems;
accompanied by the subtle element, it has the form of a shadow, is indestructible and indivisible, possesses the nature of the vajra-body, and is immutable.
The untainted state—

freed from all latent impressions of the afflictions and having attained mastery over desires— is accomplished as a form consisting of supreme bliss, like a fish leaping from water or one awakened from sleep. That which...

The one whose nature consists of name-and-form is Mahāvajradhara. Because he is liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra, he is called "liberated. [He himself is liberation, which is the union (yuganaddha).
This very sequence of emergence is [taught] in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Mahāyogatantra*.

All the Tathāgatas praise it: "O Vajra! O Vajra! O Vajra! How wonderful is this teaching of the Vajra, wherein where there is no body, speech, or mind, there form is manifested!"—as stated in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* concerning the youth Candraprabha.

The body of the Tathāgata has also been described as being equal to space, stainless, possessing the most excellent form, bodiless, characterized by signless wisdom, a son of the Sugatas, an ocean of profound qualities, and compassionate.
As it is said in the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā*: "Place your hand upon my head; there is no image [there]."
I say that nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream; if there were any dharma more distinguished than nirvāṇa, I would also say that it is like an illusion and like a dream. That...

And that non-abiding nirvāṇa is liberation, which is called "yoked-in-pair" (yuganaddha). Now, regarding its very characteristic: having understood the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate, he who knows their union as it truly is—that wise one knows reality. [This concerns] existence and nirvāṇa.
That which proceeds once unity has been realized, and wherein the two conceptual constructions are abandoned, they call that "yoked together" (yuganaddha).
When there is no conceptualization such as "selflessness of phenomena" or "selflessness of persons," that is the state of union;

and that is the imperishable station of yogins. Having understood that the with-aspect and the without-aspect are non-different, in brief, where there is no distinction between these two, they call that [the state of union].

The state of union (*yuganaddha*): having realized the perfect integration of wisdom and means, wherever that proceeds, there the supreme yogins speak of the "state of union. Where there is neither pure nor impure in any way—that which is the single assembly (*samāja*) of those two—[that is the state of union].
It would be the state of union (yuganaddha). The imagined and the dependent exist not as two distinct forms.
Where unity exists, that is this "yoked pair" (yuganaddha). This very method is non-abiding gnosis, nirvāṇa, the embodiment of supreme bliss,
as well as perfect buddhahood, the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, and the completion stage (niṣpannakrama).

It is said: "The vajra-like samādhi is also described as being like an illusion; for indeed, such expressions are recited in the sūtras, tantras, and kalpas. All those words [arising] from cessation are indicators of this, and the yogin who abides in this [state is indicated by them]."

Established in the sequence of the yoke-fastening, he is indeed called a knower of reality, a seer of illusion, and the sustainer of the universe. Likewise, established in the method of the two truths, he is the embodiment of gnosis,
the Buddha whose nature is wisdom and means, who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, who has accomplished what was to be done, and is a great yogin.

The one who discerns existence and non-existence, perfectly awakened through the Net of Illusion, the omniscient leader of the world—this reality is to be personally realized; it is the union of the two truths. Those who...

Those fools who know [otherwise] have fallen away from the teaching of the Lord of Sages. Nothing new has been written here, nor has anything been composed by my own intellect with a collection of beautiful words; rather, having seen this very [work], I have merely made it clear for the eyes.
This very [teaching] is for those who, in this world, lack the capacity to attain it.

"O Teacher, this other fault of mine should be forgiven because of its insignificance; for even the distraction of the learned is but a form of laziness. Speaking thus to his Guru, if I have cultivated any complete merit by collecting the incomparable principles of the masters as seen in many treatises, by that—

May the Victorious One, having gradually entered the state of luminosity through his victory over the hosts of enemies that are the Māras, protect the worlds! The *Vajrācāryanayottama* is completed. This work is by the Maṇḍalācārya and Paṇḍita Rāhulaguptapāda.
For the Tathāgata has spoken of both these and their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma; [homage] to the Guru Kamalavajra...
